aristotle-eudaimonia: Eudaimonia is Aristotle's name for the good life, often translated as flourishing rather than mere happiness. It is not a fleeting feeling but the condition of living well and doing well overall: exercising our distinctively human capacities, especially reason, in excellent activity over a complete life. Many scholars hold that on Aristotle's view eudaimonia requires virtue but can also need external goods such as friends, health, and luck.
aristotle-golden-mean: Aristotle's doctrine that each moral virtue lies at a midpoint between two vices: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and wastefulness, proper anger between irascibility and servility. The mean is not a mechanical average but what practical wisdom identifies as fitting, the right emotion toward the right person at the right time for the right reasons. What counts as intermediate depends on the situation.
aristotle-virtue-ethics: Virtue ethics, whose classic source is Aristotle, asks not what rules must I follow but what kind of person should I become. A virtue is a stable excellence of character, such as courage, honesty, or generosity, built through practice until acting well comes naturally. On this view, morality is chiefly about cultivating good character and living a flourishing life, rather than only weighing duties or calculating consequences.
care-ethics: The ethics of care is a moral outlook, developed by feminist thinkers such as Carol Gilligan, that puts relationships, empathy, and response to particular people's needs at the center of morality. It arose from the observation that standard moral theories prize abstract, impartial rules while neglecting the contextual, emotionally attuned reasoning that sustains families and friendships. On this view, caring for concrete others is itself a core moral competence.
care-ethics-noddings: Nel Noddings's version of care ethics makes the caring relation, one person attending to and responding to another's needs, the very foundation of morality, prior to principles or rules. Morality grows, on her account, out of natural caring, like a parent for a child, and out of memories of being cared for. Controversially, she holds that our obligations extend mainly to those we can actually reach and help.
das-man: In Heidegger's Being and Time, das Man, often translated the They, names the anonymous public one that quietly dictates how things are done, what is interesting, and what one should think. Living absorbed in these borrowed answers is what Heidegger calls inauthenticity; authenticity means taking over one's own existence and owning one's choices. He insists das Man is a structural feature of everyday life, not mere sheepish conformity.
eternal-recurrence: Nietzsche's eternal recurrence is a thought experiment: imagine your life, exactly as it has been, repeating again and again forever, every joy and every pain included. Nietzsche offered it as a test of one's relation to life. Could you affirm it so completely that you would will its endless return? Whether he meant it literally is debated; saying yes goes with his ideal of loving one's fate.
existence-precedes-essence: Sartre's slogan that existence precedes essence means human beings have no pre-set nature or purpose, unlike a knife designed before it is made. We first exist, thrown into the world without a blueprint, and then define ourselves through our choices and actions. With no fixed human essence to appeal to, we are, on this view, radically free and fully responsible for what we make of ourselves.
existentialism: Existentialism is a loose family of nineteenth- and twentieth-century philosophies, including Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus, united less by shared doctrine than by attention to lived existence: freedom, choice, anxiety, death, and the search for meaning in a world that supplies none ready-made. Existentialists typically hold that meaning and value are not handed down but must be chosen or created, and that we cannot escape this responsibility.
feminism: Feminism, as a philosophical movement, holds that women have been and remain systematically subordinated, and it criticizes the ideas, institutions, and everyday practices that sustain this. It spans many strands, from liberal feminism's fight for equal rights to radical analyses of patriarchal power and care-focused and queer approaches. Its insight that the personal is political extends the critique into marriage, housework, and intimacy, not just law and the workplace.
kierkegaard-despair: For Kierkegaard, despair is not just hopelessness but a sickness in the self: a wrong relation to oneself, whether by wanting to be someone else, refusing to become anyone, or defiantly trying to be one's own foundation. He argues the self is a balancing of finite and infinite, and that most people are in despair without knowing it. His remedy: resting transparently in the power that established you.
kierkegaard-stages: Kierkegaard distinguishes three stages, or spheres, of existence. The aesthetic life pursues pleasure, novelty, and immediacy, and collapses into boredom and despair. The ethical life chooses commitment: duties, marriage, steady obligations to others. The religious life, entered by a leap of faith, relates the individual directly to God as the absolute. Kierkegaard presents these stages through vivid pseudonymous characters rather than as dry theory.
language-games: In Wittgenstein's later philosophy, a language game is a patterned activity, such as greeting, ordering food, telling a joke, or praying, into which words are woven. The meaning of a word is not some object it labels but its use within such practices, and language as a whole is a family of overlapping games rather than one uniform system. Understanding others may therefore require sharing their way of life.
leap-of-faith: The leap of faith, in Kierkegaard, is the passionate commitment by which a person accepts religious faith, or an ultimate value, beyond what reason and evidence can settle. His model is Abraham, who trusted God by virtue of the absurd even when commanded to sacrifice Isaac, the act morality forbade. The leap is not a jump into arbitrariness but a wholehearted act of the individual will.
moral-psychology: Moral psychology studies the mind behind moral judgment and action: how character forms, why people act against their own better judgment (weakness of will, or akrasia), how emotion and reason interact, and how moral understanding develops from childhood on. Sitting between philosophy and psychology, it asks what virtues, vices, self-control, and moral responsibility actually look like in human beings, not in idealized rational agents.
parmenidean-being: The pre-Socratic Parmenides argued that nothing cannot exist or even be coherently thought, so reality must be one single, unchanging, eternal Being, and the change and variety we perceive must be illusion. His student Zeno defended the view with famous paradoxes purporting to show motion is impossible. The argument has shaped metaphysics ever since, standing behind every debate about whether change, emptiness, or plurality is ultimately real.
plato-cave: Plato's allegory of the cave imagines prisoners chained facing a wall, taking the shadows projected before them for reality itself. One prisoner is freed, painfully climbs toward the sunlight, and comes to see the real world, which for Plato is the realm of truth and the Good. Education, on this picture, is turning the soul toward what is real; the returning knower often meets hostility.
plato-forms: Plato's theory of Forms holds that beyond the changing, imperfect things we see there exist eternal, perfect exemplars, such as Beauty itself and Justice itself, of which sensible things are only imperfect copies. Genuine knowledge, on this view, is knowledge of the Forms rather than of fleeting appearances. The theory grounds Plato's distrust of mere imitation, including art, and his claim that those who grasp the Forms should rule.
socratic-ignorance: At his trial, Socrates claimed his only wisdom was knowing that he did not know the things others confidently claimed to know. This disciplined awareness of one's own ignorance is the starting point of inquiry, since pretended knowledge blocks learning. It powers the Socratic method: relentless questioning that tests beliefs until their holders discover for themselves how little they have examined them.
teleological-suspension: In Fear and Trembling, Kierkegaard argues that Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac suspended ordinary morality, the duty not to kill, for the sake of a higher, personal duty to God. This is the teleological suspension of the ethical: the single individual standing above the general law only through an absolute relation to the divine. It remains deeply troubling; many, following Kant, insist no divine command could ever override morality.
the-look: In Sartre's philosophy, the Look is the experience of being seen by another person: under someone's gaze you become an object in their world, fixed, judged, no longer a free subject. This is the idea behind his famous line that hell is other people. Yet the Look cuts both ways: it also reveals the other as an equally free consciousness who can never be fully captured or known from outside.
the-tao: The Tao, or the Way, is the central idea of Taoism: the unnameable source and pattern of all things, the way the universe naturally goes. For Confucians, by contrast, the Tao is the proper way of human life, ritual, virtue, right social order. Taoist teaching counsels yielding to the natural flow rather than forcing against it. The Tao that can be told, the Daodejing opens, is not the eternal Tao.
unexamined-life: At his trial, Socrates declared that the unexamined life is not worth living, meaning that a human life needs critical examination of one's beliefs, values, and choices to be fully worthwhile. The remark makes philosophy a way of life rather than a technical subject. It is a demanding ideal, not a description: plenty of unreflective lives go on, and some doubt such deep self-knowledge is even possible.
wu-wei: Wu wei, a central Taoist ideal, is often translated effortless action or non-action: acting in accord with the natural flow of things rather than forcing, straining, or meddling from the ego. It is not passivity; the skilled cook or craftsman whose technique has become second nature moves fluently and without friction. The Daodejing applies it even to government: rule like cooking a small fish, with minimal intervention.
